doc.title: Skitch Henderson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Milford, Connecticut, October 31, 1998

chapter: New York Pops and later work
title: Writing for strings and swing: the Whiteman violin arrangements
summary: Strings cannot swing; the orchestra could not play old Whiteman arrangements Pizzarelli found.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I don’t mean to keep bringing up Manny again, but he talked about that too, about trying to write for strings and make them swing, and he basically said don’t bother.

No. You’re wasting your time. I had a wonderful experience — Bucky found, Bucky Pizzarelli found a gentleman who is now 96 years old or something, a black violinist from the south, I think he lived in Carolina or someplace. And Paul Whiteman had heard him play, and Paul Whiteman was a genius businessman. And he heard him play and he called in one of his myriad arrangers who sat at his elbow, and they wrote arrangements on standards for four violins, traps, utility percussion, bass — we can’t tell, it’s probably one or two guitars, and piano. Wonderful, wonderful arrangements. And Bucky, the gentleman, when Bucky was on the road with Stephane Grappelli, he brought this case of music to him, so Bucky brought it back to me and we looked at it and I said, “You know when I have you or maybe when I have some time players with this orchestra, I’m going to take the two concertmasters and two principals from the second stand, let’s read them through” you know because we thought we’d discovered something that would be wonderful. They couldn’t play it. Could not play it. I mean they could play the notes, but it was just an absolute colossal disaster. It made me think how creative, I don’t know, the word jazz doesn’t apply to me, I’m such a jazz fan, but how wonderfully, the virtuosity of great jazz players. Because that’s what they were, all of them.
